opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think hardware is one of the most underappreciated parts of the story. If you look back even five or six years, robot hardware was a huge bottleneck. The robots were extremely expensive, often hundreds of thousands of dollars for a capable humanoid or a good dexterous hand, and they were fragile. They broke all the time. As a researcher, you spent more time repairing the robot than actually running experiments, which makes it really hard to iterate quickly or collect data at any meaningful scale.

What's changed in the last couple of years is that the hardware has gotten dramatically better and dramatically cheaper at the same time. You now have humanoids and robot arms that are more reliable, have better actuators, better sensing, better dexterity, and the price points are coming down toward something like the cost of a car rather than the cost of a house. That matters enormously, because robotics is fundamentally a data problem. Unlike language models, where you can scrape the internet, robot data has to be collected in the physical world, and you can't scale data collection if each robot is a delicate, one-of-a-kind machine.

So I see the hardware improvements as the substrate that makes everything else possible. Better and cheaper hardware means more robots deployed, more teleoperation data, faster iteration loops, and that feeds directly into training foundation models for robotics. It's a bit like how GPUs had to get good enough before deep learning could take off. The algorithms and the compute were necessary, but you also needed the physical platform to be ready. And I think we're finally hitting that point, where the hardware is good enough that the bottleneck shifts to the brain, to the models, and that's a problem we know how to scale.

r002.rationale: It identifies better dexterity as a recent improvement in humanoids and robot arms, communicating improved hand dexterity in context.

r003.rationale: It says current humanoids and robot arms are more reliable, communicating improved reliability of the robots as a whole.

fable-5.1.text:
Great question. I think people underestimate how much the hardware side has quietly matured over the last few years, and that matters because for a long time robotics was bottlenecked on the body, not the brain.

Take humanoids. If you tried to build a humanoid ten years ago, you were looking at something like Atlas from Boston Dynamics, which was a hydraulic machine that cost a fortune, could barely be maintained outside a lab, and you certainly couldn't buy one. Now you have multiple companies shipping electric humanoids where the cost has come down by an order of magnitude or more. The actuators are better, the motors are more power-dense, the batteries last long enough to do real work, and the whole thing is much more robust. A robot used to break after a few falls. Now you can knock it over, it gets up, and you keep going.

The reason that matters so much for AI is that it changes the economics of data collection. Foundation models in language got where they are because the internet existed and text was essentially free to collect. Robotics never had that. Every demonstration had to be collected by a human teleoperating a physical machine, and if that machine is expensive and fragile, you can't scale. When hardware becomes cheap and reliable, you can put dozens or hundreds of robots in a facility, run them for hours a day, and start approaching the kind of data volume where these large models actually begin to generalize.

The other thing is form factor convergence. If everyone builds a slightly different robot, every lab's data is incompatible with every other lab's data. Humanoids give you a common embodiment that fits a world built for humans, with the same doors, the same stairs, the same tools, so the data and the models become more shareable. And on top of that, simulation has improved alongside the hardware, so you can generate huge amounts of synthetic experience and then transfer it onto a body that behaves closely enough to the simulated one that the transfer actually works.

So it's really a confluence. The AI side finally has models that can absorb large amounts of multimodal data, and the hardware side finally gives us bodies that are affordable, durable, and consistent enough to generate that data at scale. Neither alone would have been enough. Together, that's why it feels like the field has momentum again.

r002.rationale: It describes better actuators, motors, and batteries, but does not identify improved hand dexterity.

r003.rationale: It describes robots as more robust and says they can be knocked over, get up, and keep going, communicating improved whole-body reliability.

astra-6.text:
I think hardware is finally getting to a point where it can support the ambitions we have on the AI side. Robots are becoming more capable, more reliable, and less expensive. That changes what you can actually experiment with.

If a robot is fragile or requires constant maintenance, you spend a lot of your time keeping it running instead of teaching it new skills. With better hardware, you can collect more data, run more experiments, and test whether a learned behavior works in the physical world.

And cost matters enormously. If only a few labs can afford a platform, progress is constrained. As hardware becomes more accessible, more people can work on the intelligence. So I see hardware improvements as an enabler: they give us a much better foundation for turning advances in AI into robots that can do useful things.

r003.rationale: It mentions greater reliability in general, but does not identify improved whole-body reliability.

sol-6.1.text:
I think hardware is finally getting to a point where it can support the kind of learning we want to do. You need robots that are reliable, affordable, and capable enough to collect data and try things repeatedly. If every experiment requires a lot of maintenance, it’s very hard to scale learning.

And there’s a feedback loop here. Better hardware lets you collect more data; more data helps you train better models; better models make that hardware more useful. So the renewed momentum isn’t just about AI getting smarter. It’s also about having physical platforms that let us put that intelligence to work.
